sections.text:
Autonomous driving fundamentally demands dense understanding of visual, semantic, and geometric information, yet existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are typically trained with sparse supervision such as language instructions or trajectory signals.

This direct mapping from dense visual observations to sparse representations forces the model to compress or even discard critical scene information essential for safe driving.

We argue that this limitation does not stem from insufficient model capacity, but from the lack of explicit mechanisms that encourage the formation of dense world representations in the latent space.

In this spirit, we propose a novel paradigm for driving intelligence, Think Densely, Act Sparsely, and instantiate it with an efficient and interpretable framework, LECDrive (Latent Expert Cognitive Chains for Vision-Language-Action autonomous Driving).

The core idea is to mimic the hierarchical perception process of humans by embedding a progressive chain of latent expert cognition within the VLA model.

Concretely, we inject a compact set of task-specific latent tokens as carriers, enabling the model to internalize dense knowledge from foundational vision models, including visual representations (DINOv3), semantic structures (SAM3), and spatial geometry (DepthAnything3), while maintaining efficient inference.

This interdependent cognitive chain follows a curriculum learning principle, where supervision is progressively structured from representation to semantics and geometry.

Extensive experiments demonstrate that LECDrive consistently improves the performance of base VLMs across multiple autonomous driving benchmarks, covering key tasks such as object perception, state prediction, and trajectory planning.

These findings suggest that constructing dense world models through structured latent expert chains is a promising direction for VLA-based autonomous driving.

summary.en: The paper argues that vision-language-action models for autonomous driving often receive sparse supervision, which can cause them to compress or discard scene information relevant to safe driving. It proposes the “Think Densely, Act Sparsely” paradigm and implements it as LECDrive, using task-specific latent tokens in a progressive cognitive chain to incorporate visual, semantic, and geometric knowledge. The authors report consistent improvements over base vision-language models across multiple driving benchmarks, including object perception, state prediction, and trajectory planning.

Recent advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World Action Models (WAMs) have expanded the manipulation and whole body capabilities of individual robots. Yet a single robot remains limited by its embodiment, and many real world tasks require capabilities that can only emerge through cooperation.

Existing multi robot frameworks largely emphasize task decomposition, allocation, and replanning, while providing limited support for adapting executable coordination when physical execution deviates from the intended behavior. We present CoEvolve, a framework that represents team coordination as executable code over fixed robot motor skills.

CoEvolve introduces Verifier Guided Coordination Evolution, where a multimodal foundation model instantiates coordination strategies through motion primitives, semantic objectives, temporary robot roles, and bounded execution parameters.

Physical verification evaluates each executed transition, rejected behaviors trigger structured coordination revision from an accepted checkpoint, and verified experience is retained to guide subsequent decisions. We evaluate CoEvolve with two simulated Unitree G1 humanoids transporting a freely supported rigid payload through constrained corridors.

Across 15 base task runs with three multimodal backbone families, CoEvolve completes 8 tasks, with every backbone achieving end to end success.

Additional evaluations yield verified placement on two additional corridor layouts and after both same-backbone and cross-backbone experience initialization, while exposing persistent limitations in motion precision and contact stability.

These results support executable coordination as a practical interface for adapting long horizon multi robot collaboration under shared physical constraints.

summary.en: CoEvolve represents multi-robot coordination as executable code built from fixed motor skills and revises strategies based on physical verification. The authors evaluate it in simulation with two Unitree G1 humanoids transporting a rigid payload through constrained corridors. Across 15 base runs and three multimodal backbone families, the system completes eight tasks, with every backbone achieving end-to-end success. Additional simulated evaluations show verified placement on two other corridor layouts and with same- or cross-backbone experience initialization. The authors also report persistent limits in motion precision and contact stability.

sections.text:
Recent advances in multimodal models have enabled GPT-6 Astra to perform robotic manipulation through in-context learning. Yet contact-rich control and tactile perception are often regarded as strengths of specialist policies, leaving open whether Astra can directly understand and use tactile observations.

We provide, to our knowledge, the first demonstration that Astra directly interprets vision-based tactile images and uses their contact cues for manipulation. Tactile RGB images enter through its existing visual interface, enabling few-shot closed-loop control on nineteen simulated UniVTAC and OpenViTac tasks with 210 sampled scene seeds per setting.

With visuo-tactile input, Astra achieves mean success rates of 93.8% and 81.8%, exceeding the strongest reported specialist baselines in our comparison by 22.9 and 13.1 percentage points, respectively. Vision-only performance also leads these baselines, reaching 76.3% and 80.6%.

Trajectory analysis reveals active probing, cautious grasping, contact-guided alignment, and recovery, alongside difficulties with tangential loading and corrective execution. Our findings challenge the exclusivity of specialist policies in contact-rich manipulation and show that fine-grained vision can partially compensate for missing touch.

They also identify vision-based tactile sensing as an interface for scaling contact understanding with foundation models and reveal signs of benchmark saturation. These results motivate joint visual-tactile pretraining, harder contact-rich evaluations, and physical-robot validation.

summary.en: The authors report what they describe as the first demonstration that GPT-6 Astra directly interprets vision-based tactile images and uses contact cues for manipulation. Tactile RGB images enter through the model’s existing visual interface, enabling few-shot closed-loop control on 19 simulated UniVTAC and OpenViTac tasks, with 210 sampled scene seeds per setting. Mean success rates with visuo-tactile input are 93.8% and 81.8%; vision-only rates are 76.3% and 80.6%. Trajectory analysis shows probing, cautious grasping, contact-guided alignment, and recovery, alongside difficulties with tangential loading and corrective execution. The authors call for harder evaluations and physical-robot validation.

Robotic systems for environmental monitoring and ecological surveying in wetlands and swamps must operate across diverse terrestrial and aquatic conditions. Conventional fixed-geometry wheels cannot adapt their contact geometry to these varying conditions.

This work presents MOSS (Multimodal Origami Swamp Robot System), a compact amphibious robotic platform with 3D-printed origami wheels. The compact crank mechanism switches the wheel between contracted and expanded configurations, changing its width, body diameter, and fin orientation simultaneously.

The contracted configuration is better suited to efficient rolling on firmer ground, whereas the expanded configuration provides greater contact and terrain engagement on softer surfaces. MOSS was evaluated on soil, sand, mud with varying water content, and water, in addition to in-motion morphing and terrestrial-aquatic transition tests.

The more energy-efficient wheel configuration depended on terrain. The contracted configuration achieved a lower cost of transport on firmer soil and mud, whereas the expanded configuration performed better on wetter mud, sand, and water, reducing the cost of transport by up to 29%.

Expanded wheels also reduced slip in wet mud and reduced both slip and hub sinkage in sand. MOSS successfully completed configuration changes in $1.95 \pm 0.11$ s and demonstrated continuous locomotion across soil-mud-water transitions. Outdoor trials further demonstrated operation across natural deformable terrain and water.

These results show that adaptive wheel geometry provides terrain-dependent locomotion benefits and enables a single compact platform to traverse substantially different terrestrial and aquatic conditions.

summary.en: MOSS is a compact amphibious robot with 3D-printed origami wheels that switch between contracted and expanded configurations through a crank mechanism. The change alters wheel width, body diameter, and fin orientation. Contracted wheels suit firmer ground, while expanded wheels increase contact with softer terrain. Evaluations covered soil, sand, mud at varying water content, water, in-motion morphing, and terrestrial-aquatic transitions. The more energy-efficient configuration depended on terrain: expanded wheels performed better on wetter mud, sand, and water, reducing cost of transport by up to 29%. They also reduced slip in wet mud and slip and hub sinkage in sand. Outdoor trials showed operation across natural deformable terrain and water.

Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) pairs wrist-camera videos with camera trajectories and gripper openings, providing scalable, robot-free data for learning how bimanual actions change a shared scene.

Existing interactive world models, however, typically rely on text or single-camera control and struggle to follow each arm's actions while maintaining consistency between the two wrist views.

We introduce UMI-WM, an action-conditioned bimanual world model that jointly generates both wrist views from observation history, per-arm relative camera poses, and gripper widths, with cross-view consistency, action following, and visual fidelity.

UMI-WM injects each arm's actions into its own wrist stream, while sparse hub tokens exchange scene information between the two streams. Camera-aware geometry conditioning and camera-guided noise further support per-view motion control and cross-view geometric exchange.

We adapt the model for block-causal generation and distill the 30-step Teacher into a Student with four denoising steps. We train UMI-WM on self-collected open-world and in-studio UMI recordings combined with public manipulation data.

To evaluate action following, we use an inverse dynamics model (IDM) to recover relative camera poses and gripper widths from generated videos, and introduce Bimanual Action Fidelity (BAF) to measure how closely these recovered actions match the conditioning actions.

UMI-WM achieves the best results on all five reference-video fidelity metrics and the best or competitive performance on VBench and WorldArena. The Teacher and Student outperform all compared baselines in action following, while the four-step Student generates paired wrist videos 6.9 times faster than the Teacher.

summary.en: The paper introduces UMI-WM, a bimanual world model that generates paired wrist-camera views conditioned on observation history, per-arm relative camera poses, and gripper widths. It injects actions into each arm’s stream and exchanges scene information across streams to support action following and view consistency. The authors distill a 30-step Teacher into a four-step Student and train on collected and public manipulation data. Evaluations report top performance on five reference-video fidelity metrics and best or competitive VBench and WorldArena results; both models outperform compared baselines in action following, and the Student generates paired videos 6.9 times faster.

Tethered mobile robots can sustain long-duration operation through continuous power supply and stable communication via their cables. However, cable-environment interaction causes unintended obstacle displacement, cable snagging or entanglement, and even cable damage, leading to mission failure.

To assess the risk of individual cable-obstacle contacts, this study investigates cable tension as a sensing modality for estimating whether a contacted obstacle is movable or non-movable.

We conducted experiments with a tethered mobile robot and collected tension data while varying robot velocity, contact angle between the obstacle and cable, obstacle mass, and obstacle side-surface material.

The results show that obstacle movability is characterized by the initial tension rise and, more importantly, by whether the tension relaxes or remains high after its peak. Based on these observations, we select six features from the tension profiles and train a logistic-regression classifier using 117 labeled trials.

The proposed method distinguishes movable and non-movable cases with a balanced accuracy of 95.5% after 30 cm of post-contact travel. These results demonstrate the potential of cable tension for risk assessment of cable-obstacle interactions and provide a step toward online, cable-aware autonomous navigation.

summary.en: This study examines whether cable tension can indicate if an obstacle contacted by a tethered mobile robot is movable, helping assess risks such as snagging, displacement, or cable damage. Experiments varied robot speed, contact angle, obstacle mass, and side-surface material. The authors report that tension behavior after its peak, especially whether it relaxes or remains high, characterizes obstacle movability. They selected six features from tension profiles and trained a logistic-regression classifier on 117 labeled trials. After 30 cm of post-contact travel, it distinguished movable from non-movable cases with 95.5% balanced accuracy.

sections.text:
Developing coordination policies for complex multi-agent systems relies on either labor-intensive algorithm design or opaque task-specific reinforcement learning.

With recent advances in autonomous coding agents, we show that policy search directly in code space offers a compelling third path that combines automated optimization with explicit interpretability.

We investigate a human-directed workflow in which coding agents iteratively propose, implement, evaluate, diagnose, and eventually refine algorithms guided by simulation feedback and explicit correctness verification. We conducted two case studies and found that this workflow robustly outperformed any manually engineered solutions.

On a challenging map in the 2024 League of Robot Runners competition, a two-day search discovered a policy that exceeds the stronger locally reproduced competition entry by 35.0% on the densest instance and generalizes to unseen map instances.

In simulated real-world warehouses with irregular lanes, continuous robot geometry, and asynchronous motion, a week-long search discovered an entirely new class of multi-agent pathfinding algorithm that outperforms a calibrated proprietary solution in throughput by 58.9%.

Under stated assumptions, we further prove that the new algorithm is collision-free and completes, in finite time, every accepted goal that is not withdrawn or replaced.

Together, the studies show that policy search in code space powered by state-of-the-art coding agents offers a highly competitive path to building real engineering solutions that are both effective and analytically tractable.

summary.en: The paper studies human-directed policy search in code space, where coding agents iteratively propose, implement, evaluate, diagnose, and refine multi-agent pathfinding algorithms using simulation feedback and explicit correctness checks. In two case studies, the workflow outperformed manually engineered solutions. A two-day search produced a policy that exceeded a stronger locally reproduced 2024 competition entry by 35.0% on the densest instance and generalized to unseen maps. In simulated warehouses, a week-long search found a new algorithm class with 58.9% higher throughput than a calibrated proprietary solution. Under stated assumptions, the authors prove collision freedom and finite-time completion of accepted goals that are not withdrawn or replaced.

sections.text:
We introduce DexOAK, a learning-based object-aware kinematic retargeting framework for generating contact-consistent robot hand references from human motion-capture data.

DexOAK first minimizes an interaction-graph Laplacian objective over a joint hand-object graph, so the robot reproduces the demonstrated object-relative interaction geometry rather than the human hand pose alone.

These per-frame solutions form seed retargeted references, from which a feed-forward network conditioned on human keypoints and object point clouds learns the retargeting function.

Object-aware finetuning then refines the network under contact, non-penetration, and self-collision losses that position the fingers on the demonstrated contacts and reduce artifacts destabilizing physics-based refinement. Once trained, the network transfers to unseen data by inference alone, without per-frame optimization.

DexOAK references improve dynamic retargeting over the state-of-the-art across bimanual tasks with rigid and articulated objects. On the Inspire hand, success rises from 39.5% to 48.4% on OakInk-v2, and ADD-AUC rises from 62.7% to 77.9% on ARCTIC.

Ablations trace the gains to object-aware kinematic retargeting and the amortized network refined with contact losses. Trained on OakInk-v2, it transfers to ARCTIC zero-shot and nears in-domain performance after fine-tuning. On hardware, 46/56 open-loop replays succeed across five tasks, enabling dexterous robot data generation from human data.

Visualizations and interactive results are at: https://fspinola.github.io/dexoak/.

summary.en: DexOAK is a learning-based, object-aware kinematic retargeting framework that generates contact-consistent robot hand references from human motion-capture data. It optimizes per-frame solutions on a hand-object interaction graph, trains a feed-forward network conditioned on human keypoints and object point clouds, and fine-tunes it with contact, non-penetration, and self-collision losses. The authors report improvements over prior dynamic retargeting methods across bimanual tasks, with gains on OakInk-v2 and ARCTIC using the Inspire hand. On hardware, 46 of 56 open-loop replays succeeded across five tasks.

sections.text:
Data-driven learning for general-purpose robotic manipulation presents a fundamental trade-off between data-collection cost and adaptability to real-world environments. Imitation learning (IL) requires costly human demonstrations, whereas simulation-based learning is vulnerable to sim-to-real gaps in dynamics and sensor observations.

We propose ReDOA (Real-World Distillation via Observation Alignment), a framework that decouples control learning from perception learning to learn image-based policies in the real world.

A state-based teacher policy trained in simulation is executed on a real robot, and its control knowledge is distilled into an image-based student policy using the collected trajectories. Observation Alignment resolves observation mismatches between data collection and deployment.

This framework collects successful, efficiently executed trajectories paired with real-world visual observations, without requiring demonstrations from human experts.

In real-robot experiments on three non-prehensile manipulation tasks, including bimanual manipulation, our method achieves better overall performance when jointly considering task success and execution efficiency than both IL based on human demonstrations and policy distillation in simulation. https://isri-aist.github.io/redoa-project-page/

summary.en: ReDOA aims to learn image-based manipulation policies in real-world settings while addressing data-collection costs and observation mismatch. A state-based teacher trained in simulation runs on a real robot, and its control knowledge is distilled into an image-based student using collected trajectories. Observation Alignment addresses differences between observations during collection and deployment. The authors say this approach gathers successful, efficiently executed trajectories without human expert demonstrations. In real-robot experiments on three non-prehensile tasks, including bimanual manipulation, it performs better overall than human-demonstration imitation learning and simulation-based policy distillation when success and execution efficiency are considered together.

sections.text:
Robotic rearrangement tasks require planning sequences of actions that fulfill high-level specifications while also being geometrically feasible. Symbolic abstractions make the combinatorial structure of rearrangement tasks tractable, but they usually do not fully capture the geometric constraints that determine which actions a robot can actually realize.

These constraints are hard to express in the symbolic model. We propose REAP (Rearrangement with Elicited Action Preconditions), a framework in which a relational graph neural network heuristic is learned over a simple symbolic abstraction. A motion planner serves as a supervisor that elicits the hidden geometric preconditions of the problem during training.

Deployed with greedy best-first search, the learned heuristic generalizes out-of-distribution along object count, plan length, and object arrangement, and can be trained jointly on several domains.

Compared to classical heuristic search and learning-based baselines, REAP solves more problems, requires roughly an order of magnitude fewer motion-planner queries than comparable methods, and the action it ranks first is geometrically feasible in 94% of sampled states, against 22% for a random choice.

summary.en: REAP learns rearrangement heuristics from motion-planner feedback to address geometric feasibility constraints that simple symbolic models do not capture. A relational graph neural network operates over a symbolic abstraction, while a motion planner supervises training by eliciting hidden action preconditions. The learned heuristic is deployed with greedy best-first search. The authors report out-of-distribution generalization across object count, plan length, and arrangement, as well as joint training across domains. Compared with classical heuristic search and learning-based baselines, REAP solves more problems, uses roughly an order of magnitude fewer planner queries than comparable methods, and ranks a feasible action first in 94% of sampled states.

sections.text:
Tactile perception is crucial for precise robotic manipulation, providing an important foundation for dexterous, closed-loop force control. Among various tactile sensing techniques, magnetic tactile sensors stand out thanks to their fine-grained, three-dimensional force perception capability and strong robustness against visual occlusion.

In this study, we discover a physical loophole called PhantomTac in magnetic tactile sensors. The attacker can alter the magnetic field, thus spoofing the force interpreted by magnetic tactile sensors.

The attacker can stealthily deploy such an attack by simply attaching a thin (the thickness is around 0.5 mm), battery-free magnetic tag to the surface of an object. Hence, the attack tag can be easily concealed by a barcode sticker. Such an attack scheme is "deploy-and-forget" -- the attacker can deploy the tag and leave.

When a robotic hand is picking up an object, it may severely damage the object. Specifically, spoofing the normal force can crush the object, whereas spoofing the shear force can lead to a loose grip, thus dropping the object.

Compared with directly sabotaging the robotic hand, PhantomTac is much more concealed as the attacker does not need access to the device. We performed extensive reverse-engineering efforts to characterize the sensing mechanism of commercial-off-the-shelf tactile sensors and proposed a practical tag design.

End-to-end evaluations conducted on real robots and robotic arms demonstrate that our attack can bypass existing anti-interference mechanisms and effectively hijack their closed-loop control processes, achieving an attack success rate exceeding 95% when the grasping-position offset is bounded within 8 mm.

Finally, based on the limitations of existing anti-magnetic interference mechanisms, we propose a multimodal-consistency defense mechanism to mitigate such physical-layer security threats.

summary.en: The paper presents PhantomTac, a physical vulnerability in magnetic tactile sensors that lets an attacker spoof perceived force by altering the magnetic field. A thin, battery-free tag attached to an object can be concealed under a barcode sticker and left in place. During grasping, spoofed normal force may crush an object, while spoofed shear force may loosen the grip. Reverse engineering and end-to-end evaluations on real robots and robotic arms are reported; the authors state that success exceeds 95% when grasp-position offset is within 8 mm and that the attack bypasses existing interference defenses. They propose multimodal-consistency defense.

sections.text:
Changes in a robot's observations do not automatically imply changes in the task it is solving, but language-conditioned manipulation systems often fail to separate the two. If an object moves, for example, the locations at which actions should be executed may change while the underlying manipulation plan remains valid.

We introduce Sequential Planning via Anchored Robotic Keypoints (SPARK), which separates a task's symbolic plan from its execution-time perceptual grounding, and we experimentally isolate whether a fixed symbolic plan can survive substantial changes to the scene through execution-time re-grounding.

SPARK represents the task as a symbolic behavior tree whose object references are grounded to current 3D observations during execution, allowing the robot to update where actions are performed while preserving the plan. Runtime verification then enables local recovery and renewed grounding, only resorting to a new plan if necessary.

To test the separation between plan and perceptual-grounding, we perform a set of manipulation experiments with a fixed plan while moving objects during execution. Under a 10 cm displacement, verification and adaptation maintain $66.7\%$ task success, compared with $2.2\%$ when disabled, demonstrating the importance of the underlying principle.

Without task-specific model training and with an open-weight planner, SPARK also achieves $66.8\%$ mean success across six LIBERO-PRO settings, and $68\%$ across eleven physical task-embodiment settings on three robot platforms.

Together, these results show that robustness does not require re-planning the task and for an important class of failures, it is sufficient to preserve the plan and update the system's perception of a changing world. Code and videos can be found at \url{https://cwru-aism.github.io/spark-page/}

summary.en: SPARK separates a task’s symbolic plan from its execution-time perceptual grounding. In manipulation experiments that move objects during execution, a fixed plan with verification and adaptation achieves 66.7% task success under a 10 cm displacement, compared with 2.2% when these mechanisms are disabled. The authors also report mean success of 66.8% across six LIBERO-PRO settings and 68% across eleven physical task-embodiment settings on three robot platforms.

sections.text:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models show promising knowledge accumulation ability through pretraining, yet continual learning remains challenging. Existing continual imitation learning (CIL) methods often require additional parameters or modules, limiting scalability for large VLA models.

We propose Stellar VLA, a knowledge-driven CIL framework without parameter growth, featuring two variants: T-Stellar for task-centric modeling and TS-Stellar for hierarchical modeling of reusable skills across tasks.

Stellar VLA jointly optimizes task representations and a self-evolving knowledge space, with knowledge-posterior-guided expert routing using knowledge relations and Top-K semantic embeddings for task specialization. Experiments on LIBERO demonstrate strong performance against VLA and CIL baselines with only 1% replay.

Dual-arm real-world experiments validate knowledge transfer across embodiments and scenes. TS-Stellar excels in hierarchical manipulation, while visualizations demonstrate knowledge retention and task discovery. Project Website: https://stellarvla.github.io/

summary.en: The paper proposes Stellar VLA, a continual imitation learning framework for vision-language-action models that aims to accumulate skills without increasing parameter count. It includes T-Stellar for task-centric modeling and TS-Stellar for hierarchical modeling of reusable skills across tasks. The framework jointly optimizes task representations and a self-evolving knowledge space, using knowledge relations and semantic embeddings to guide expert routing. In LIBERO experiments, the authors report strong performance against VLA and continual-learning baselines with 1% replay. Dual-arm real-world experiments evaluate knowledge transfer across embodiments and scenes; TS-Stellar is reported to excel at hierarchical manipulation.

sections.text:
Reinforcement learning enables learning high-performance control policies, but its reliance on extensive interaction limits deployment on physical systems where data collection is costly, and failures are unsafe.

We introduce Prior-Informed Adaptation (PIA), an offline-to-online model-based RL framework that uses structured simulation priors for rapid adaptation. PIA pretrains a world model on heterogeneous low- and high-fidelity simulated trajectories, then adapts it with limited target-domain interaction using uncertainty-regularized planning.

Rather than requiring an accurate simulator for policy transfer, PIA treats simulated trajectories as biased priors whose residual mismatch is corrected during online adaptation. We evaluate PIA in autonomous racing using high-fidelity simulation and on a real full-size autonomous race car.

In simulation, PIA adapts faster across track and surface shifts than strong baselines, achieving lower lap times and fewer failures. On hardware, PIA achieves reliable few-shot adaptation with less than one hour of on-vehicle interaction.

summary.en: The paper presents Prior-Informed Adaptation (PIA), an offline-to-online model-based reinforcement learning framework. It pretrains a world model on simulated trajectories of varying fidelity, then adapts through limited target-domain interaction and uncertainty-regularized planning. The authors treat simulated data as potentially biased priors whose mismatch is corrected online. In autonomous-racing simulation, PIA adapts faster than strong baselines across track and surface shifts, with lower lap times and fewer failures. On a real full-size race car, they report reliable few-shot adaptation using less than one hour of vehicle interaction.

sections.text:
Experience generated during deployment offers an opportunity for robots to improve policy reliability through learning from their own executions. However, learning through human corrections requires teleoperators to monitor execution and intervene when policies fail, a demand that is difficult to meet as robot fleets grow.

We introduce collective experience learning (CEL), a learning paradigm in which deployed robots share their execution experience to improve a common policy.

We realize CEL through failure-guided experience retrieval fine-tuning (FERT), which uses failure contexts from robot executions to retrieve relevant trajectory segments from the fleet's shared successful experience and uses their actions as supervision for policy updates, without collecting additional expert demonstrations or corrective actions.

A fault-tolerant asynchronous training system (FATS) coordinates experience collection, policy optimization and policy distribution despite local interruptions within the robot fleet.

Across five real-world manipulation tasks, the resulting policies achieve success rates of 93.3-99.2%, evaluated over 120 trials per task on robots excluded from training data collection. With collection time per robot held fixed, larger fleets provide more experience and FERT generally achieves higher success rates across the evaluated sizes.

On multi-stage phone packaging, learning with 96 robots increases success from 79.2% to 98.3%.These results support collective experience as a practical basis for scalable robot learning and a path towards improving policy reliability during deployment without collecting additional expert corrective actions.

summary.en: The paper introduces collective experience learning (CEL), in which deployed robots share execution experience to improve a common policy. Its implementation, failure-guided experience retrieval fine-tuning (FERT), retrieves relevant successful fleet trajectories from failure contexts and uses their actions to supervise policy updates, without additional expert demonstrations or corrections. A fault-tolerant asynchronous system coordinates collection, training, and distribution. Across five real-world manipulation tasks, the authors report success rates of 93.3–99.2% on robots excluded from training data collection. Larger fleets generally perform better when collection time per robot is fixed; in phone packaging, 96 robots raise success from 79.2% to 98.3%.

sections.text:
Contact-rich manipulation is essential to everyday activities, yet evaluating robots' ability to perform these activities remains challenging because of their diverse contact behaviors and the difficulty of reproducing tasks across laboratories.

Drawing on observations of everyday human manipulation, we identify eight recurring skill categories that provide a practical framework for studying these capabilities. We introduce ContactBench 1.0, an extensible benchmark that instantiates these skills through 36 reference tasks and more than 40 object assets.

The assets capture task-relevant geometry and contact behavior, support reproducible fabrication using consumer-grade 3D printers, and are paired with simulation models with tunable resistance loads. Controlled task variations enable evaluation of policy generalization.

We evaluate recent vision-based and vision-tactile policy learning methods on six benchmark tasks. The results reveal that the evaluated vision-only policies struggle to perceive or react to contact events, while the evaluated visual-tactile policies do not meaningfully improve performance.

By providing shared tasks and physical and simulated assets, ContactBench 1.0 establishes a foundation for reproducible evaluation of contact-rich manipulation research. The benchmark is open-sourced at https://jingyi-xiang.github.io/contactbench

summary.en: The paper presents ContactBench 1.0 for evaluating contact-rich robotic manipulation in everyday activities. Based on observations of human manipulation, it defines eight skill categories and provides 36 reference tasks and more than 40 object assets. The assets capture task-relevant geometry and contact behavior, support fabrication with consumer-grade 3D printers, and pair with simulation models whose resistance loads can be tuned. Evaluation on six tasks finds that the tested vision-only policies struggle with contact events, while the tested vision-tactile policies do not meaningfully improve performance.

sections.text:
Vision-language-action (VLA) policies must ground language instructions in the right objects, contact points, and target locations for reliable manipulation. Human gaze provides a natural signal for this grounding, but existing robot datasets rarely pair real human gaze with the multi-camera observations used by modern policies.

We introduce GazeAct, a gaze-equipped real-robot manipulation dataset and training framework for multi-view VLA policies.

Using screen-based teleoperation, we record gaze directly on the robot camera feed viewed by the operator, yielding 12000 demonstrations across 40 tasks and five domains with 300 Hz gaze synchronized with images, proprioception, and actions.

We transfer gaze from the operator-selected view to the remaining synchronized cameras, producing spatially consistent targets across the policy's visual inputs. We then use these gaze-derived targets to regularize language-conditioned visual attention during training while keeping inference gaze-free.

Across 18 real-world tasks, our method improves average success from 48.1% to 58.6%, with gains up to 25 percentage points. Ablations show that gaze works best as soft supervision and that real human gaze provides stronger attention targets than generic attention-shaping priors.

The gains transfer to LIBERO-Spatial (57.9% to 69.6%) and different VLA backbones.These results show that gaze collected in the robot observation space can provide effective training-time targets for improving visual grounding in VLA manipulation.

summary.en: The paper introduces GazeAct, a real-robot manipulation dataset and training framework for multi-view vision-language-action policies. Operators’ gaze is recorded on robot camera feeds during screen-based teleoperation and transferred to synchronized views. The resulting targets provide soft supervision for language-conditioned visual attention during training, while inference remains gaze-free. The authors report improved success rates across 18 real-world tasks and on LIBERO-Spatial, with gains also transferring across different policy backbones.
summary.zh: 论文介绍 GazeAct，一个面向多视角视觉—语言—动作策略的真实机器人操作数据集与训练框架。研究通过屏幕遥操作记录操作员在机器人相机画面上的注视，并将注视目标迁移至同步的其他视角，用作训练时语言条件视觉注意力的软监督，推理时无需注视输入。作者报告，该方法在18项真实任务及LIBERO-Spatial上提升成功率，并适用于不同策略骨干。

sections.text:
Reference-image-conditioned video generators are increasingly used as neural simulators for embodied planning and policy learning, yet their ability to anticipate physical hazards is rarely evaluated.

We introduce ICAT, which grounds test construction in incident reports and safety guidance through structured risk memories, constrained case generation, and human verification. The resulting benchmark contains 909 evaluation units with explicit initial conditions, triggering actions, and documented consequences.

Across six generation systems, severe outcomes are frequently missing or attenuated even when the initial state is preserved and the risky action is executed: the strongest system achieves 23.5% conditional strict success under best-of-eight selection.

Expert auditing, image-generator sensitivity analysis, matched safe-risky pairs, and alternative-outcome scoring provide complementary checks on this system-level finding. ICAT exposes a gap between reproducing risky actions and generating their documented consequences.

summary.en: The paper presents ICAT, a method for testing physical-risk prediction in embodied world models using incident reports and safety guidance. It constructs evaluation cases through structured risk memories, constrained generation, and human verification. Across six video-generation systems, severe consequences were often missing or weakened even when the initial state and risky action were preserved. The strongest system reached 23.5% conditional strict success under best-of-eight selection. Additional audits and analyses provide complementary checks on this system-level finding.
summary.zh: 论文提出 ICAT，一种以事故报告和安全指南为依据的具身世界模型物理风险预测测试方法，通过结构化风险记忆、受约束案例生成和人工核验构建评测单元。对六种视频生成系统的评估显示，即使初始状态保留且执行了风险动作，严重后果也常被遗漏或弱化；最强系统在 best-of-eight 选择下的条件严格成功率为23.5%。专家审查等分析为这一系统层面的发现提供补充检验。

sections.text:
Translating language into humanoid motion requires coordinating body parts, determining motion duration, and producing references suitable for robot execution. We introduce PartiGen, a part-aware latent diffusion framework that incorporates anatomical structure into a shared whole-body motion representation.

Part-specific attention processes anatomically masked frame features, and its outputs are fused to combine local limb information with whole-body context. Conditioned on text and motion history, the model generates motion primitives autoregressively.

Forward-kinematics supervision encourages kinematic consistency, while a learned end-of-sequence predictor selects a frame-level endpoint after generation. On HumanML3D retargeted to the Unitree G1, PartiGen achieves a segment-level FID of 3.165, a 16.8% reduction over TextOp, and improves R@1 by 1.4 percentage points.

In the duration study with 16-frame primitives, endpoint prediction reduces mean absolute duration error from 12.471 to 3.080 frames compared with a fixed-length cutoff. We further evaluate robot execution using a pretrained, frozen GRIT tracker: 409 of 500 generated references (81.8%) pass the posture-based stability screen in MuJoCo.

Following simulation screening and manual selection, 26 of 27 attempted motions are judged successful on the real G1.

summary.en: The paper introduces PartiGen, a part-aware latent diffusion framework for language-conditioned humanoid motion generation. It combines limb-level features with whole-body context and autoregressively generates motion primitives from text and motion history. Forward-kinematics supervision supports kinematic consistency, and a learned predictor selects the endpoint. On HumanML3D retargeted to the Unitree G1, the authors report better segment-level FID than TextOp. Endpoint prediction reduced duration error in a study using 16-frame primitives. Simulation screening and real-robot attempts were also evaluated.
summary.zh: 论文提出 PartiGen，一种用于语言条件人形机器人动作生成的部位感知潜在扩散框架，将局部身体部位信息与全身上下文结合，并依据文本和动作历史自回归生成动作片段。模型采用正向运动学监督，并预测生成终点以确定动作时长。在 HumanML3D 转换至 Unitree G1 的评估中，作者报告其片段级 FID 优于 TextOp；时长研究中，终点预测降低了平均绝对时长误差。MuJoCo稳定性筛查及真实机器人尝试结果也有报告。

sections.text:
Dynamical system (DS)-based learning from demonstration generates flexible robot motions, but existing guarantees rely on certificate generation to obtain formal guarantees of safety and goal convergence.

We propose a symbolic supervisory control architecture that automatically generates a fail-safe backup plan, certifying safety, reachability, and actuator feasibility directly from the robot's dynamics, independent of the learned DS.

A nominal controller tracks the learned DS, while the supervisory controller monitors safety and target convergence, providing non-conservative intervention when the nominal controller violates necessary constraints.

Experimental results include simulations and real robot deployment with various 2D and 3D datasets, including handwriting datasets, validating the effectiveness of our approach in providing formal guarantees with learned motion even in complex, dynamic environments.

summary.en: The paper proposes a symbolic supervisory control architecture for formally certifying robot motions learned from demonstrations. It generates a fail-safe backup plan directly from robot dynamics and certifies safety, reachability, and actuator feasibility independently of the learned dynamical system. A nominal controller tracks the learned motion, while a supervisor monitors safety and goal convergence and intervenes when required constraints are violated. The authors report simulations and real robot deployments using varied 2D and 3D datasets, including handwriting, as evidence of effectiveness in complex dynamic environments.

sections.text:
Multi-UAV exploration is often constrained by unreliable communication, limited field-of-view sensing (e.g., lightweight onboard camera), and finite travel budgets that require each robot to reserve enough budget to return to its base.

We present Dec-MARVEL, a decentralized, communication-free exploration policy that jointly selects waypoints and sensing headings from each robot's local map, remaining budget, and opportunistic observations of teammates.

Across 900 held-out trials spanning three team sizes (2, 4, 8 robots) and three travel budgets (720, 800, and 1024 m) against four baselines, Dec-MARVEL achieves the highest or tied-highest exploration and success rates and the shortest reported travel to 99% merged coverage among successful trials in all nine budget--team configurations.

Under our tightest 720 m budget, it reaches 46%, 84%, and 94% success for 2, 4, and 8 robots, versus 17%, 57%, and 85% for the strongest baseline in each case. Physical-robot experiments show that the resulting waypoint-heading plans are executable and remain budget-feasible.

summary.en: The paper presents Dec-MARVEL, a decentralized, communication-free multi-UAV exploration policy. Each robot selects waypoints and sensing headings using its local map, remaining travel budget, and opportunistic observations of teammates, while reserving enough budget to return to base. Across 900 held-out trials covering nine combinations of team size and travel budget, the authors report the highest or tied-highest exploration and success rates, and the shortest reported travel to 99% merged coverage among successful trials. Physical-robot experiments show the plans are executable and budget-feasible.
summary.zh: 本文提出 Dec-MARVEL，一种无需通信的多无人机分布式探索策略，根据各机器人的局部地图、剩余行程预算及对队友的机会性观察，联合选择航点与感知朝向，并为返航预留预算。作者在三种队伍规模、三种行程预算组成的九种配置中，对 900 次留出试验与四种基线进行比较；报告称该方法的探索率和成功率最高或并列最高，且成功试验中达到 99% 合并覆盖所需行程最短。实物机器人实验显示规划可执行且符合预算。

sections.text:
For natural human-robot interaction, a robot must understand human intent expressed not only through language but also through nonverbal signals such as gestures and gaze. However, current robot policies rely on language instructions as the sole interface for conveying intent, leaving nonverbal signals unused and placing the full burden of communication.

In this work, we present EDITH, a robot framework that captures the human's nonverbal signals through continuous streams of first-person view and gaze from smart glasses, and uses them alongside language instructions as inputs to the robot policy.

Our hardware system streams the human's first-person view, gaze, and speech to the robot in real time, transcribing the speech into language instructions.

To handle these rich but noisy signals, we design a hierarchical policy in which a high-level policy infers the human's intent and produces a sequence of subtasks, where each subtask is represented as a fine-grained instruction paired with a keyframe that grounds the intent in the scene (e.g., the frame where the human points at the target object).

A low-level policy then executes these subtasks. In our experiments on human-robot interactive tasks, EDITH enables the robot to act on the human's nonverbal signals even when intent is expressed only briefly, and significantly reduces user effort to convey intent compared to using language instructions alone.

Visit our project page for source code and real-robot demo videos.

summary.en: The paper presents EDITH, a robot framework that combines language instructions with first-person vision and gaze captured by smart glasses. The system streams the human’s view, gaze, and speech to the robot and transcribes speech into instructions. Its hierarchical policy infers intent at a high level and produces subtasks, each represented by a fine-grained instruction and a scene-grounding keyframe; a low-level policy executes them. In human-robot interaction experiments, the authors report that EDITH responds to briefly expressed nonverbal signals and reduces user effort compared with language-only instructions.

sections.text:
World Action Models (WAMs) jointly predict robot actions and future observations. However, their visual prediction objectives do not explicitly distinguish task-relevant transitions from incidental scene changes. For whole-body policies, this distinction matters because task progress depends on coordinated changes in body pose, contact, and object state.

We introduce LANGUAGE-FORCING, a training strategy that uses language to emphasize task-relevant changes in the future visual representations of a whole-body WAM. Given paired current and ground- truth short-horizon future frames, a frozen vision-language model assesses task progress and predicts plausible subsequent state changes.

We encode these descriptions with a frozen text encoder and align their embeddings with intermediate, action-conditioned future-visual features, complementing the original visual and action prediction objectives. All auxiliary components are used only during training, introducing no additional inference overhead.

On HumanoidArena, LANGUAGE-FORCING achieves an average success rate of 79.17%, exceeding the strongest competing policy by 9.46 percentage points and the same WAM without language alignment by 10.77 percentage points. Across five real-world tasks, language alignment raises average success from 53.33% to 71.33% over the same WAM baseline.

summary.en: The paper proposes LANGUAGE-FORCING, which uses language signals to guide a whole-body world action model toward future visual changes relevant to task progress. Frozen vision-language and text encoders provide auxiliary alignment during training, with no added inference overhead. The authors report a 79.17% average success rate in HumanoidArena, above the strongest competing policy and the same model without language alignment. Across five real-world tasks, average success also rises over that model’s baseline.
summary.zh: 论文提出 LANGUAGE-FORCING，用语言信号引导全身世界动作模型关注与任务进展相关的未来视觉变化，并将冻结视觉语言模型和文本编码器用于训练阶段的特征对齐；这些辅助组件不会增加推理开销。作者报告，在 HumanoidArena 仿真中，方法平均成功率为 79.17%，高于最强对比策略及未对齐语言的同一模型；五项真实世界任务的平均成功率也高于该模型基线。

sections.text:
Classical robot control, Finite State Machines and Behavior Trees (BTs), is deterministic and inspectable but fixed at design time: it fails on situations its designers did not anticipate. Foundation models can synthesize new control logic at runtime, at a cost in latency and non-determinism hard to accept in safety-critical aerial systems.

Existing LLM-driven approaches keep the model in the loop permanently and discard what it produces. We propose Self-Crystallizing Behavior Trees (SCBT), in which the foundation model is a compiler rather than a runtime.

When a BT node fails, an LLM proposes a minimal, mission-agnostic subtree patch; CMA-ES tunes its parameters in simulation; a contextual bandit decides whether a stored patch or a new LLM call is worth its cost; and a three-stage admission pipeline (static check, invariant-monitored replays, an empirical margin over the unpatched tree) admits only patches that demonstrably recover.

Admitted patches are stored in a fleet library and, once the LLM call rate decays, crystallized into a deterministic BT that no human wrote. We implement SCBT on Microsoft Project AirSim with a schema-constrained LLM pipeline (Gemini 3.1 Pro) and a lockstep simulator.

Over three seeds of a 20-episode learning phase with wind-gust and battery failures, SCBT used $11\pm1.4$ LLM calls against 26 for whole-tree regeneration and 22 without a library, with 0.33 calls per episode in the second half.

The crystallized trees, 28 and 33 nodes with two patches each, reached $97\pm2\%$ mission success with no learning running, against 12\% for the unpatched tree and 98\% for a hand-coded expert tree, and reproduce decision traces exactly when re-ticked offline.

Two negative results: replay admission rejected useful wind recoveries by attributing wind-induced geofence excursions to the patch, and a static-only ablation generalized better to held-out failures.

summary.en: The paper proposes Self-Crystallizing Behavior Trees (SCBT), where a foundation model proposes mission-agnostic subtree patches after node failures. Simulation tunes patch parameters, and a contextual bandit plus a three-stage admission process filters them. Accepted patches enter a fleet library and can form deterministic trees that run without the model. In Project AirSim simulations with wind and battery failures, the authors report fewer learning-phase model calls than two baselines and 97±2% mission success for crystallized trees without ongoing learning, near a hand-coded expert tree. They also report rejected useful patches and better held-out generalization in a static-only ablation.
summary.zh: 论文提出自结晶行为树 SCBT：基础模型在行为树节点失败时提出任务无关的子树补丁，参数经仿真优化，再由上下文赌博机和三级准入流程筛选；通过的补丁存入机队库，最终形成无需运行基础模型的确定性行为树。作者在 Project AirSim 的风扰和电池故障仿真中报告，学习阶段调用量低于两种对照方案，结晶树在不继续学习时达到 97±2% 任务成功率，接近手写专家树。研究也报告了有用补丁被误拒及静态检查消融泛化更好的负面结果。

sections.text:
World models (WMs) and world-action models (WAMs) focus on future world prediction and executable action generation, respectively. Although these models learn shared physical dynamics and interaction semantics from embodied trajectories, they are typically trained in isolation, which restricts knowledge reuse between prediction and control.

The central challenge is therefore to develop a unified learning framework that shares these dynamics while preserving the distinct modeling capabilities required by each paradigm. We propose UniW(A)M, a mixture-of-experts world-(action) model built upon diffusion Transformers that unifies action-conditioned world modeling and diverse WAM variants.

Shared experts capture common dynamics, while atomic capability experts are reused across interfaces so that each interface keeps its own conditional pathway.

At deployment, a plug-in adaptive interface router (PAIR) learns from a small subset of target-task chunk scenarios to select a suitable WAM interface for each execution chunk, balancing task success and execution efficiency while keeping the backbone frozen.

We evaluate UniW(A)M on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and three real-world manipulation tasks, where it achieves 88.3% average real-world success versus 76.7% for the strongest baseline. On WorldArena, it leads action-conditioned world modeling on all three tasks.

AC-WM co-training contributes to action generation on every action interface and PAIR raises OOD success from 63.3% to 76.7%.

summary.en: The paper proposes UniW(A)M, a diffusion Transformer mixture-of-experts framework that unifies action-conditioned world modeling with several world-action model variants. Shared experts represent common dynamics, while reusable capability experts preserve distinct interface pathways. At deployment, PAIR selects a WAM interface for each execution chunk using a small set of target-task scenarios, with the backbone frozen. The authors report results on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, real-world manipulation tasks, and WorldArena, as well as gains attributed to co-training and PAIR.
summary.zh: 论文提出 UniW(A)M，一个基于扩散 Transformer 的混合专家框架，旨在统一动作条件世界建模与多种世界—动作模型。共享专家表征共同动力学，原子能力专家跨接口复用，同时保留各接口的条件路径。部署时，PAIR 根据少量目标任务片段场景为每个执行片段选择 WAM 接口，并保持骨干网络冻结。作者报告其在 LIBERO、RoboTwin 2.0 和三项真实操作任务上的平均成功率高于最强基线，在 WorldArena 的三项任务上领先；摘要还称联合训练和 PAIR 带来动作生成与分布外成功率方面的提升。

sections.text:
Reducing actuator count simplifies robot hardware but also removes independent inputs for maneuvering. The original Rollbot steered by modulating a quasi-stable helical orbit, but moved slowly and relied on external motion capture.

Rollbot 2 preserves the single-actuator design while its redesigned mass distribution enables near-straight rolling and more direct travel toward commanded paths and beacon targets. Onboard inertial and ultra-wideband sensing support learned steering, beacon seeking, and waypoint following through one motor-velocity command.

Rollbot 2 autonomously approaches UWB beacons without motion capture and completes a 468~m manually commanded indoor route at 0.87~m/s. On the shared 4.8~m ``N'' waypoint benchmark, all 16 trials complete the path with a mean traversal time of 10.8~s and mean time-averaged deviation of 7~cm.

Its fastest traversal takes 8.0~s, over 70 times faster than the original Rollbot's 564~s run despite minor protocol differences. These results show how mechanical redesign, onboard sensing, and learning-based control improve the agility and autonomy of a single-actuator spherical robot.

summary.en: The paper presents Rollbot 2, a spherical robot that retains a single actuator. A redesigned mass distribution supports nearly straight rolling, while onboard inertial and ultra-wideband sensing enable learned steering, beacon seeking, and waypoint following through one motor-velocity command. The abstract reports autonomous beacon approach without motion capture, completion of a manually commanded indoor route, and results on a shared waypoint benchmark. The authors attribute improvements in agility and autonomy to mechanical redesign, onboard sensing, and learning-based control.
summary.zh: 论文介绍 Rollbot 2，一种保留单执行器设计的球形机器人。重新设计的质量分布使其能够近似直线滚动，并利用机载惯性与超宽带传感器，通过单一电机速度指令实现学习式转向、信标搜寻和路径点跟随。摘要称，该机器人无需外部运动捕捉即可自主接近超宽带信标，并完成室内路线及共享路径点基准测试。作者据此认为，机械设计、机载感知和学习控制提升了单执行器球形机器人的灵活性与自主性。

sections.text:
Robotic systems with revolute joints evolve on circular state spaces, yet most control architectures represent these states using Euclidean variables that ignore this underlying geometry.

We propose a fully spiking neural control architecture in which ring attractors encode joint states, enforcing representations consistent with the topology of revolute systems.

Homeostatic regulation computes goal-state mismatch directly over these distributed representations, and opponent gain-modulated populations convert this mismatch into controlled phase shifts of the activity bump, implementing set-point regulation as motion on the ring.

We show that the bump dynamics follow an SO（2） geometry, and that gain asymmetries induce a signed phase velocity on the ring. To interface distributed activity with scalar regulation signals, we derive an analytic Fourier phase decoder and implement its signed components using push-pull spiking populations.

For multi-joint systems, we demonstrate that local ring-based Fourier features compose into product representations that linearly decode SO（3） orientations through forward kinematics. Experiments in NEST validate the full SO（2） regulation mechanism and the spiking product-feature decoder for lift, pitch, and yaw.

Robot experiments on a Tiago arm show that decoded ring dynamics generate joint velocity commands, producing directed motion with joint-dependent accuracy.

Together, these results establish a neuromorphic control framework in which representation, regulation, and action are unified within a ring-attractor substrate aligned with the geometry of revolute systems.

summary.en: The paper proposes a fully spiking neural architecture for revolute-joint robot control, using ring attractors to encode joint states in a way aligned with their circular topology. Homeostatic regulation computes goal mismatch over distributed representations, while gain-modulated populations shift the activity bump’s phase. The authors derive an analytic Fourier phase decoder and describe how multi-joint features compose into representations that linearly decode SO(3) orientations. NEST experiments validate the SO(2) regulation mechanism and decoder; Tiago arm experiments show directed motion from decoded joint-velocity commands, with accuracy varying by joint.
summary.zh: 论文提出一种用于旋转关节机器人控制的全脉冲神经架构，以环吸引子编码关节状态，使表示符合圆形状态空间的拓扑。稳态调节机制直接计算目标状态与分布式表示之间的差异，并通过增益调制群体控制活动峰的相位移动。作者推导解析傅里叶相位解码器，并展示多关节特征如何组成可线性解码 SO(3) 姿态的乘积表示。NEST 实验验证了 SO(2) 调节机制与解码器；Tiago 机械臂实验显示，解码动态可生成关节速度指令并产生方向性运动，准确度因关节而异。

sections.text:
Animals build cognitive maps of vast environments, use them to perform map-based navigation, and might even be reusing the same circuitry used in spatial reasoning for creating and using maps of arbitrary task-spaces.

In contrast, current embodied AI systems either rely on hand-engineered mapping pipelines, which break in the presence of unmodeled dynamics and are restricted to metric space, or on learned policies that rarely form map-like representations at all.

Developing architectures that could learn to build and use map-like representations as flexibly as animals is, however, difficult because few embodied AI benchmarks actually require map-based reasoning.

To address this, we present ForagerSim --- an interdisciplinary research platform and simulation environment focused on embodied tasks that require map-based reasoning, with scenarios ranging from mobile-robot search and rescue to animal foraging in both complex mazes and vast, potentially infinite open areas.

ForagerSim is highly modular and allows modifying independent axes of difficulty related to perception (abstract 2D sensing to full RGB or LiDAR), scale (room-scale to multi-km scale), topology (open-fields to complex mazes), dynamics (smoke, debris, sensorimotor failures and others) and tasks (from simple 2D coverage to foraging-inspired well-alternation tasks).

We compare reinforcement learning baselines with a simple engineered robotics stack and a human player on 8 example worlds which show how different difficulty axes affect existing methods.

Our results show that, when sensing is simplified to 2D, learned policies can perform multi-object search and well-alternation tasks surprisingly well in simple topologies, but they fall short of human performance in larger or more complex-topology environments where map-based baselines perform well, suggesting that map-based reasoning is the bottleneck in these scenarios.

summary.en: The paper introduces ForagerSim, a modular simulation platform for embodied tasks requiring map-based reasoning, including robot search and rescue and animal foraging. Its difficulty can vary across perception, scale, topology, dynamics, and task type. In eight example worlds, the authors compare reinforcement-learning baselines, an engineered robotics stack, and a human player. With simplified 2D sensing, learned policies perform well in simple topologies but trail humans in larger or more complex environments.
summary.zh: 论文提出 ForagerSim，这是一个面向具身地图推理任务的模块化仿真平台，场景涵盖机器人搜救与动物觅食，并可调整感知、规模、拓扑、动态因素和任务类型。作者在八个示例世界中比较强化学习基线、工程机器人方案和人类玩家。结果显示，在简化为二维感知且拓扑简单时，学习策略能完成多目标搜索和交替觅食；在更大或拓扑更复杂的环境中，其表现低于人类，而地图推理基线表现良好。作者据此认为这些场景的瓶颈是地图推理。

sections.text:
Flow-matching vision-language-action (VLA) models generate an action chunk by iteratively denoising Gaussian noise, but typically execute only a short prefix before replanning with updated observations. Under this receding-horizon paradigm, the unexecuted remainder---the action tail---is discarded, and the next chunk is regenerated from fresh noise.

We show that this discarded tail retains transferable denoising progress: action-tail initialization can match or outperform a native 10-step Gaussian baseline using fewer denoising steps. However, the optimal denoising budget varies substantially across samples, indicating that tail reuse should be adapted to the updated environment.

Based on this observation, we introduce VLA-Rolling, a lightweight inference framework that reuses action tails through three stages: action-tail inheritance, per-action confidence estimation, and confidence-guided refinement through renoising and denoising budget allocation, while the underlying VLA remains frozen.

Across $\pi_{0.5}$, SmolVLA, X-VLA, and MolmoAct2 on LIBERO, MetaWorld, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0, VLA-Rolling reduces action-chunk inference cost in all 16 model--benchmark pairs, achieving up to a $1.48\times$ speedup, while improving success rate in 14 pairs by up to $15.08$ percentage points.

These results show that action tails are not merely discarded predictions, but reusable intermediate states that enable more efficient and accurate VLA inference. These results demonstrate that the action tail can support the generation of better actions with fewer denoising steps. Our project is available at https://chenbao123ww.github.io/VLA-Rolling/.

summary.en: VLA-Rolling is a lightweight inference framework that reuses the unexecuted action tail of a vision-language-action model. It inherits the tail, estimates confidence per action, and guides refinement through renoising and denoising-budget allocation while keeping the underlying model frozen. Across 16 model-benchmark pairs, the authors report reduced inference cost in every pair, with speedups up to 1.48×, and higher success rates in 14 pairs.
summary.zh: 论文提出 VLA-Rolling，一种在视觉语言动作模型推理中复用未执行动作尾部的轻量框架。它继承动作尾部、估计各动作的置信度，并据此通过重新加噪和分配去噪步数进行调整，同时保持底层模型冻结。作者在四种模型和四个基准上的16组组合中评估，报告推理成本均下降，最高加速1.48倍；14组成功率提高，最高增加15.08个百分点。

sections.text:
Learning inertial odometry for a new platform usually requires ground-truth trajectories.

We show that an inertial odometry model can instead be trained from scratch by a myopic teacher that integrates the IMU over each short window independently, a scheme we call integration self-supervision.Interestingly, although supervised only by short-window velocity changes, the student learns to directly predict velocity, and does so more accurately than its integration teacher.

Pose graph distillation then refines the model with sequence-consistent targets from a pose graph over many windows. Training on a new platform therefore no longer requires collecting ground-truth trajectories, but only calibrating the IMU and recording data during normal operation.

Across six datasets spanning pedestrians, drones, quadrupeds, and a humanoid, the same recipe with no velocity or position labels trains models that come within $0.07$~m/s average velocity error of a same-architecture supervised baseline.

summary.en: The paper presents an inertial-odometry training method that uses no velocity or position labels. A teacher integrates IMU data independently over short windows to provide self-supervision, followed by pose-graph distillation for sequence-consistent targets. The authors report that the student directly predicts velocity more accurately than its integration teacher. Across six datasets covering pedestrians, drones, quadrupeds, and a humanoid, its average velocity error comes within 0.07 m/s of a same-architecture supervised baseline.

sections.text:
Robotic manipulation in agricultural environments remains challenging due to variations in plant geometry, occlusion, and camera viewpoints. Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) and generalist robot policies offer a promising approach to addressing these challenges by learning manipulation behaviors from multimodal observations and language instructions.

However, adapting these policies to agricultural tasks requires domain-specific demonstrations, which are costly and time-consuming to collect on physical robots. In this work, we develop a simulation-to-real robot-learning framework for agricultural reaching and grasping that integrates task-specific demonstration collection and pretrained policy adaptation.

A MuJoCo-based agricultural environment is developed with diverse tomato plant structures to support demonstration collection and controlled evaluation. Expert demonstrations are collected through joystick teleoperation, with a low-level controller used to execute robot actions.

Two pretrained generalist robot policies, Octo and $\pi_{0.5}$, are adapted using simulated demonstrations, followed by further fine-tuning on a physical Franka Research 3 manipulator using real-robot demonstrations.

The adapted policies are evaluated under in-distribution, viewpoint/spatial-shift, and out-of-distribution conditions in simulation, followed by physical-robot experiments. The influence of proprioceptive information on policy performance is also investigated.

Results show that $\pi_{0.5}$ achieves higher task-performance scores than Octo and exhibits less degradation under distribution shifts. These findings demonstrate the potential of integrating pretrained generalist policies with task-specific demonstration learning for agricultural manipulation.

summary.en: The paper studies adapting pretrained generalist robot policies to agricultural reaching and grasping. The authors build a MuJoCo tomato-plant environment, collect expert demonstrations through joystick teleoperation, adapt Octo and π0.5 with simulated demonstrations, and further fine-tune them using demonstrations from a physical Franka Research 3. Evaluation covers simulated in-distribution, viewpoint or spatial-shift, and out-of-distribution conditions, followed by physical-robot experiments. The reported results give π0.5 higher task-performance scores and less degradation under distribution shifts than Octo.

sections.text:
Achieving autonomous and versatile whole-body loco-manipulation remains a central barrier to making humanoids practically useful.

Yet existing approaches are fundamentally constrained: retargeted data are often scarce or low-quality; methods struggle to scale to large skill repertoires; and, most importantly, they rely on tracking predefined motion references rather than generating behavior from perception and high-level task specifications.

To address these limitations, we propose ULTRA, a unified framework with two key components. First, we introduce a physics-driven neural retargeting algorithm that translates large-scale motion capture to humanoid embodiments while preserving physical plausibility for contact-rich interactions.

Second, we learn a unified multimodal controller that supports both dense references and sparse task specifications, under sensing ranging from accurate motion-capture state to noisy egocentric visual inputs.

We distill a universal tracking policy into this controller, compress motor skills into a compact latent space, and apply reinforcement learning finetuning to expand coverage and improve robustness under out-of-distribution scenarios. This enables coordinated whole-body behavior from sparse intent without test-time reference motions.

We evaluate ULTRA in simulation and on a real Unitree G1 humanoid. Results show that ULTRA generalizes to autonomous, goal-conditioned whole-body loco-manipulation from egocentric perception, consistently outperforming tracking-only baselines with limited skills.

summary.en: The paper presents ULTRA, a unified multimodal framework for humanoid whole-body loco-manipulation. It uses physics-driven neural retargeting for motion-capture data, distills a universal tracking policy into a controller, compresses skills into a latent space, and applies reinforcement-learning fine-tuning. The controller accepts dense references or sparse task specifications and supports sensing from motion-capture state to noisy egocentric vision. In simulation and on a Unitree G1, the authors report autonomous goal-conditioned behavior from perception and consistent gains over tracking-only baselines with limited skills.

Lifelong robot learning requires acquiring new tasks sequentially without forgetting earlier ones. With large pre-trained vision-language-action (VLA) backbones, adapter-based methods effectively mitigate this challenge.

However, their task-specific adapters and selection modules accumulate with the task stream, creating a scalability challenge in on-disk storage and deployment cost under fixed onboard resource budgets.

We propose SARAM, a lifelong learning framework that limits storage growth while keeping GPU memory and per-step inference cost independent of the task stream length.

For each new task, SARAM reuses frozen adapters from previous tasks and introduces new adapters only at sparsely selected layers, with a duplication penalty encouraging them to capture information not already represented by the adapter library.

At deployment, a compact signature derived from backbone activation statistics identifies the task once per episode, and the corresponding task update is merged into the backbone, leaving only the backbone in the control loop. Across four LIBERO suites, SARAM matches or exceeds adapter-based baselines while adding up to 4.5x less on-disk state per task.

GPU memory usage and control frequency remain comparable to those of the backbone as the task stream grows. Experiments on a real UR5 arm with a different backbone further demonstrate retention throughout a sequential task stream.

summary.en: The paper introduces SARAM to limit adapter storage growth in lifelong robot learning with vision-language-action backbones, while keeping GPU memory and per-step inference cost independent of task-stream length. For each new task, it reuses frozen adapters and adds new ones only at sparsely selected layers, with a penalty encouraging novel information. At deployment, a signature from backbone activation statistics identifies the task once per episode, and its update is merged into the backbone. Across four LIBERO suites, SARAM matches or exceeds adapter baselines with up to 4.5 times less on-disk state per task. A real UR5 experiment reports retention across sequential tasks.

sections.text:
Visual navigation requires goal directed planning informed by predictions of environment dynamics. Representative navigation world model methods propose complete action candidates before predicting consequences for selection or search updates. For each candidate, predictions primarily evaluate proposed actions rather than guide its stepwise construction.

To this end, we propose InJepa, an intention first planning paradigm centered on latent states. A goal conditioned JEPA proposes latent intentions, and an action conditioned JEPA continually predicts future latent states. Both operate in a shared latent space to align their predictive representations.

Within each candidate, predicted consequences feed into the next intention proposal and action inference, forming a closed loop of intention, action, and consequence. This extends the world model's role beyond evaluation to leading candidate construction through latent intentions. We evaluate InJepa through closed loop image goal navigation in Habitat MP3D.

The results show effective multistep navigation through intention guided action generation and consequence feedback. Experiments across encoders further support applicability across visual representations.

These findings support latent intentions as the central planning object and show that world models can directly guide plan construction through coordinated reasoning about intentions and consequences. Code is available at https://github.com/zhuxun132/InJepa.

summary.en: The paper presents InJePA, a visual navigation planning method centered on latent intentions. A goal-conditioned JEPA proposes intentions, while an action-conditioned JEPA predicts future latent states; both operate in a shared latent space. Within each candidate plan, predicted consequences feed into subsequent intention proposals and action inference, creating a loop that uses the world model to construct plans step by step. Closed-loop image-goal navigation evaluation in Habitat MP3D reports effective multistep navigation through intention-guided action generation and consequence feedback. Experiments across encoders support applicability across visual representations.

sections.text:
Passive-wheel quadrupedal robots offer energy-efficient locomotion through leg-driven propulsion and momentum-driven gliding. However, navigation requires coordinating steering with intermittent propulsion and adapting push-glide timing to task demands.

Velocity-tracking objectives may suppress the speed variations inherent in skating, discouraging efficient gliding. To address these challenges, we propose SkateNav, a unified skating-navigation framework based on reinforcement learning.

A time-budgeted goal-reaching objective allows the policy to jointly learn steering, propulsion, and their temporal allocation. An adaptive skating cycle structures gliding, pushing, and recovery, while frequency modulation at every control step adjusts phase durations to navigation demands.

Simulation experiments demonstrate higher average success rates and lower cost of transport than the evaluated planner-controller baselines, with ablations confirming the contributions of cycle structure and frequency adaptation.

Real-world experiments demonstrate zero-shot transfer from simulation to a passive-wheel Mini Cheetah across cluttered indoor spaces, slopes, and paved outdoor surfaces. Supplementary videos are available on the project page: https://ktw1404.github.io/SkateNav/

summary.en: The paper introduces SkateNav, a reinforcement-learning framework for skating navigation on passive-wheel quadrupedal robots. It jointly learns steering, propulsion, and their timing, using an adaptive skating cycle and stepwise frequency modulation. In simulation, it achieves higher average success rates and lower cost of transport than the evaluated planner-controller baselines; ablations support the roles of cycle structure and frequency adaptation. Real-world experiments show zero-shot transfer to a passive-wheel Mini Cheetah tested in cluttered indoor spaces, on slopes, and on paved outdoor surfaces.
summary.zh: 论文提出 SkateNav，一种面向被动轮四足机器人的强化学习滑行导航框架，联合学习转向、推进及其时间分配，并通过自适应滑行周期和逐控制步频率调节来适应导航需求。仿真显示，相较所评估的规划器与控制器基线，其平均成功率更高、运输成本更低；消融实验支持周期结构和频率自适应的作用。真实机器人实验显示，该方法可从仿真零样本迁移至 Mini Cheetah，并在室内杂乱环境、斜坡和铺装户外地面进行测试。

sections.text:
Long-range throwing on unstructured terrain is a key capability for mobile robots in delivery and retrieval tasks, but it requires high release velocity, coordinated whole-body motion, and robustness to terrain-induced disturbances.

We present a whole-body kinetic-coordination framework for a wheeled-quadruped manipulator that combines kinetic-chain arm modeling with SQP-based trajectory optimization and a reference-guided reinforcement learning policy for coordinated base motion.

The manipulator is first reduced to a kinetic-chain model and optimized under kinematic and dynamic constraints to produce a high-speed throwing reference. On a stationary base, the optimized arm trajectory reaches a release speed of 12.75 m/s and a throwing distance of 16.68 m.

When whole-body coordination is enabled, the system further increases the release speed to 16.64 m/s and the throwing distance to 28.25 m. We then integrate the mobility of the wheeled-quadruped platform and validate the complete policy through hardware experiments on flat ground, grass, slopes, and rough roads.

The results show that kinetic-chain optimization and whole-body coordination together enable robust long-range throwing across diverse unstructured terrains.

summary.en: The paper presents a whole-body kinetic-coordination framework for long-range throwing with a wheeled-quadruped manipulator. It combines kinetic-chain arm modeling, SQP-based trajectory optimization, and a reference-guided reinforcement-learning policy for base motion. On a stationary base, the optimized arm trajectory reaches a release speed of 12.75 m/s and a distance of 16.68 m; with whole-body coordination, these rise to 16.64 m/s and 28.25 m. Hardware experiments cover flat ground, grass, slopes, and rough roads, and the authors report robust throwing across these terrains.
